text.p: Westpac Banking Corp's bid for Bank of Melbourne Ltd was finally cleared by Australian authorities on Friday after four months of deliberations.
The A$1.44 billion deal needed approval from monopolies watchdog, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Treasury.

As a condition of ACCC approval, Westpac agreed to preserve Bank of Melbourne's brand and autonomy as well giving Victorian customers of smaller deposit taking institutions access to its teller machines and its electronic payments network.

Westpac made its bid in April, offering A$9.75 a share for Bank of Melbourne, including a 90 cents fully franked special dividend with the balance of A$8.85 to be paid in cash or as one Westpac share and up to A$1.85 in cash.

ACCC chairman Allan Fels said the commission had concluded the merger would not substantially lessen competition in the Victorian regional market after taking into account the effect of Westpac's undertakings.
Fels said the banking industry had changed a lot since the ACCC last looked at regional bank mergers in September 1995 when it cleared Westpac's bid for Western Australia's Challenge Bank.
"In particular, increased competition from mortgage originators have not only forced banks to cut rates sharply, but also has led to more product unbundling," Fels said.

The Commission's evaluation of the merger was based on the conclusion that although some product clustering still occurred, more consumers were shopping around amongst the different suppliers to get the best deal.

"BML has traditionally been strong in the home loan sector However, the national market for home loans is not highly concentrated and competition from non-bank financial institutions have forced interst rates down to a competitive
But Fels said the ACCC still saw signficant elements of the banking market as being regional in character.
The chairman of Bank of Melbourne, Christopher Stewart, welcomed the merger and said a meeting of shareholders would be held in late September to vote on the proposal.

"Bank of Melbourne will be combined with the Victorian retail and commercial operations of Westpac and the merged business will be carried on as Bank of Melbourne with strong local management," Stewart said in a statement.
Stewart said the bank's board believed the merger was in the best interests of shareholders, customers and staff.
"Our identity, our strong customer relationships and our high standards of cost-effective service will be adopted throughout the combined branch network," he said.
Westpac executive director John Morschel also welcomed the merger approval and said customers of both banks would benefit.
"The Bank of Melbourne name will be retained and customers can be confident the merger will bring about a stronger regional bank within a national network," Morschel said.
At 3.50 p.m (0550 GMT), Westpac shares were eight cents firmer at A$8.21, while Bank of Melbourne stock was 15.2 cents higher at A$9.81.
